Entropy Pooling (EP) is a probability-updating framework for
incorporating subjective views into an existing risk model.

Its main advantage is flexibility. The prior distribution does not need
to be Gaussian, and views can be expressed on linear or nonlinear
functions of the underlying risk factors. In Meucci's formulation, the
goal is to construct a posterior distribution that satisfies the views
while introducing as little additional structure as possible relative to
the reference model.

The central idea is remarkably simple:

> **Entropy Pooling does not change the scenarios. It changes how likely
> each scenario is.**

This idea is worth keeping in mind throughout the derivation. Most of
the mathematics below is simply a way of finding the new scenario
probabilities that satisfy the views while remaining as close as
possible to the original probabilities.

## From a prior model to weighted scenarios

Suppose the risk model contains $N$ risk factors and is represented by
$J$ historical or simulated scenarios.

We collect these scenarios in the matrix

$$X =
\begin{bmatrix}
X_1'\\
X_2'\\
\vdots\\
X_J'
\end{bmatrix},$$

where $X_j$ denotes the $j$-th joint realization of the $N$ risk
factors.

Thus,

$$X\in\mathbb{R}^{J\times N}.$$

Each scenario is associated with a prior probability. Collecting these
probabilities gives

$$p=
\begin{bmatrix}
p_1\\
\vdots\\
p_J
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
p_j\geq0,
\qquad
\mathbf 1'p=1.$$

For an equally weighted historical sample, for example, $p_j$ is

$$p_j=\frac{1}{J}.$$

More generally, the probabilities $p$ may already incorporate
information such as time decay, conditioning variables, or another
probability model.

The pair

$$(X,p)$$

therefore represents the **prior** distribution.

This is exactly the numerical representation used in Entropy Pooling: a
panel of scenarios together with their associated probabilities.

### A note on notation

Throughout this vignette, we use $q$ for the posterior probabilities.
Meucci denotes these probabilities by $\tilde p$; the change in notation
is only intended to make the distinction between prior probabilities $p$
and posterior probabilities $q$ easier to see.

A useful mental picture is therefore

$$\underbrace{(X,p)}_{\text{prior}}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\underbrace{(X,q)}_{\text{posterior}}.$$

The matrix $X$ does not change. Only its probabilities do.

## Expressing views

Views do not need to refer directly to the individual risk factors in
$X$. Instead, suppose that the investor is interested in $K$ quantities

$$V=g(X),$$

where

$$g(X)=
\left(
g_1(X),\ldots,g_K(X)
\right).$$

The functions $g_k(\cdot)$ may be linear or nonlinear. This allows views
to be expressed on quantities such as portfolio returns, spreads,
volatility, rankings, medians, quantiles, or other characteristics of
the distribution.

For each scenario $X_j$, we evaluate the functions $g_k$. This produces
a $J\times K$ matrix of view scenarios,

$$V_{j,k}=g_k(X_j).$$

The important point is that the views eventually become restrictions on
the probabilities assigned to these scenarios.

Consider a simple example. Suppose $r_j$ is the return of an asset in
scenario $j$, and the investor believes that its expected return should
equal some value $\mu_{\text{view}}$.

Under the posterior probabilities $q$, this view becomes

$$\sum_{j=1}^J q_j r_j
=
\mu_{\text{view}}.$$

Nothing has happened to the returns $r_j$. Entropy Pooling changes the
weights $q_j$ until their weighted average satisfies the view.

A bullish inequality view could similarly be written as

$$\sum_{j=1}^J q_j r_j
\geq
\mu_{\text{view}}.$$

This ability to handle both equality and inequality constraints is one
of the useful features of EP.

## Writing the views compactly

A collection of views can be represented compactly as

$$Fq\leq f$$

for inequality constraints, and

$$Hq=h$$

for equality constraints.

Here:

- $q$ is the $J\times1$ vector of posterior scenario probabilities;
- each row of $F$ represents one inequality view, while $f$ contains the
  corresponding bounds;
- each row of $H$ represents one equality constraint, while $h$ contains
  the corresponding target values.

For convenience, the normalization condition

$$\mathbf 1'q=1$$

can also be included as one of the rows of $Hq=h$.

There is no need to attach too much meaning to $F$, $f$, $H$, and $h$.
They are simply a compact way of collecting all the investor's views
into matrices and vectors.

### Notation at a glance

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:-----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------|
| $J$ | number of scenarios |
| $N$ | number of risk factors |
| $K$ | number of quantities on which views are expressed |
| $X$ | $J\times N$ matrix of prior scenarios |
| $X_j$ | $j$-th joint scenario |
| $p$ | prior scenario probabilities |
| $g(\cdot)$ | functions defining the quantities on which views are expressed |
| $V=g(X)$ | values of those quantities across the scenarios |
| $q$ | posterior scenario probabilities |
| $Fq\leq f$ | inequality views |
| $Hq=h$ | equality views, including probability normalization |
| $\lambda,\nu$ | Lagrange multipliers used to solve the optimization problem |
| $c$ | confidence assigned to the views |

The symbols will become more intuitive once we see how they interact.

## Which posterior should we choose?

Once the views have been imposed, there will generally be many
probability vectors $q$ that satisfy them.

Entropy Pooling needs a principle for choosing among them.

Meucci's answer is to choose the posterior distribution that satisfies
the views while remaining as close as possible to the prior
distribution. The measure of discrepancy used for this purpose is
relative entropy, or the Kullback--Leibler divergence.

In the discrete scenario representation, this is

$$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}
q_j
\left[
\log(q_j)-\log(p_j)
\right].$$

The quantity is zero when

$$q=p,$$

and becomes positive as the posterior probabilities move away from the
prior probabilities.

The full-confidence Entropy Pooling problem can therefore be written as

$$q^*
=
\arg\min_q
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)$$

subject to

$$Fq\leq f,
\qquad
Hq=h.$$

This is perhaps the most important equation in the entire method.

It says:

> *Among all probability distributions that satisfy my views, choose the
> one that distorts the prior probabilities as little as possible.*

If the prior already satisfies the views, no adjustment is needed and

$$q^*=p.$$

If the views conflict with the prior, the probabilities are adjusted
just enough to make the constraints hold.

The scenarios themselves remain untouched.

## What does Entropy Pooling actually do to the scenarios?

It may help to visualize the mechanism before going further.

Suppose three scenarios originally have probabilities

$$p=
\begin{bmatrix}
0.30\\
0.40\\
0.30
\end{bmatrix}.$$

Imagine that the first scenario is unfavorable for a variable on which
we have expressed a bullish view, while the third scenario is favorable.

Entropy Pooling might produce something such as

$$q^*=
\begin{bmatrix}
0.20\\
0.35\\
0.45
\end{bmatrix}.$$

The scenarios have not moved:

$$X_1,\quad X_2,\quad X_3$$

They are exactly the same observations as before.

Instead, the bullish view has made the favorable scenarios more
important and the unfavorable scenarios less important.

This is why it is often helpful to think of EP as a **scenario
reweighting procedure**. The actual optimization determines precisely
how much each scenario needs to be adjusted.

## Why solve a dual problem?

At first sight, the optimization above might look computationally
expensive.

If the risk model contains $J=100{,}000$ scenarios, then the vector $q$
contains $100{,}000$ unknown probabilities.

Fortunately, the structure of the relative-entropy objective allows us
to avoid solving directly for all of them.

Consider the Lagrangian

$$\mathcal L(q,\lambda,\nu)
=
q'
\left[
\log(q)-\log(p)
\right]
+
\lambda'(Fq-f)
+
\nu'(Hq-h),$$

where

$$\lambda\geq0$$

contains the Lagrange multipliers associated with inequality constraints
and $\nu$ contains those associated with equality constraints.

Taking the first-order condition with respect to $q$,

$$\frac{\partial\mathcal L}
{\partial q}
=
\log(q)-\log(p)
+
\mathbf 1
+
F'\lambda
+
H'\nu
=
0.$$

Therefore,

$$q(\lambda,\nu)
=
\exp
\left(
\log(p)
-\mathbf 1
-F'\lambda
-H'\nu
\right)$$

where the exponential is applied element by element.

This expression already tells us something useful: the resulting
probabilities are automatically positive.

More importantly, $q$ is now an explicit function of the multipliers
$\lambda$ and $\nu$. We can substitute this expression back into the
Lagrangian and solve the **dual problem**

$$(\lambda^*,\nu^*)
=
\arg\max_{\lambda\geq0,\nu}
D(\lambda,\nu).$$

The posterior probabilities are then recovered from

$$q^*=q(\lambda^*,\nu^*) = \exp(\log(p)-\mathbf 1 -F'\lambda^*-H'\nu^*)$$

This is the numerical trick that makes Entropy Pooling particularly
attractive.

The original problem has one unknown probability for every scenario. The
dual problem instead has roughly one unknown multiplier for every
constraint.

If there are $100{,}000$ scenarios but only five views, solving for a
handful of multipliers is much easier than directly optimizing over
$100{,}000$ probabilities.

## The conceptual picture

We can now summarize the whole procedure in one diagram:

$$\underbrace{(X,p)}_{\text{prior}}
\quad
\xrightarrow{
\substack{
\text{views on }g(X)\\
Fq\leq f,\;Hq=h
}
}
\quad
\underbrace{(X,q^*)}_{\text{full-confidence posterior}}$$

The prior risk model provides the scenarios $X$ and their original
probabilities $p$. The investor provides views.

Entropy Pooling finds the probability vector $q^*$ that satisfies those
views while minimizing the divergence from $p$.

So, in one line,

$$\text{same scenarios, different probabilities}$$

This interpretation is also important computationally. Suppose an
expensive pricing model has already transformed each risk-factor
scenario into a corresponding security-price or portfolio P&L scenario.

Since EP changes only the probabilities, those securities do not need to
be repriced. The same price or P&L scenarios can simply be analyzed
using $q^*$ instead of $p$.

## What does "confidence" mean?

So far we have assumed that the investor has **full confidence** in the
views. That is an important qualification.

The optimization

$$q^*
=
\arg\min_q D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)$$

subject to the views produces a distribution for which those views hold
completely.

But an investor may think:

> "I believe this view, but I am not willing to discard the information
> contained in my original model entirely."

Entropy Pooling handles this distinction separately.

Let

$$c\in[0,1]$$

denote the confidence assigned to the views.

The confidence-weighted posterior probabilities are

$$p_c
=
(1-c)p+cq^*.$$

This equation has a particularly intuitive interpretation.

If

$$c=0,$$

then

$$p_c=p.$$

We have no confidence in the view, so nothing changes.

At the other extreme, if

$$c=1,$$

then

$$p_c=q^*.$$

We have full confidence in the view and use the Entropy Pooling
posterior without shrinking it back toward the prior.

For intermediate values,

$$0<c<1,$$

the final distribution is a mixture of the prior model and the
full-confidence posterior.

For example, with

$$c=0.60,$$

we obtain

$$p_c
=
0.40p+0.60q^*.$$

The final model therefore gives 60% weight to the distribution implied
by the views and retains 40% of the original prior model.

This also clarifies an important distinction: **a view and the
confidence in that view are not the same thing.**

For example, one may have a view that future volatility will be high
while simultaneously having low confidence that the view will
materialize.

The first statement determines the **content of the constraint**.

The second determines **how strongly the resulting posterior should
replace the prior**.

The complete conceptual picture is therefore

$$\underbrace{(X,p)}_{\text{prior}}
\quad
\xrightarrow{
\text{views}
}
\quad
\underbrace{(X,q^*)}_{\text{full-confidence posterior}}
\quad
\xrightarrow{
\text{confidence }c
}
\quad
\underbrace{(X,p_c)}_{\text{final posterior}}$$

Or, in terms of probabilities alone,

$$p
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
q^*
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
(1-c)p+cq^*.$$

This separates the two questions that Entropy Pooling is answering:

1.  **If the views are correct, what should the distribution look
    like?**\
    This is answered by the entropy-minimization problem and produces
    $q^*$.

2.  **How much do I trust those views?**\
    This is answered by $c$, producing the final probabilities $p_c$.

That distinction is conceptually simple, but it is one of the most
useful features of the framework.

## Why is Entropy Pooling useful?

The main appeal of EP is not that it assumes a particularly convenient
statistical distribution. Quite the opposite: its strength is that very
little parametric structure is required.

The prior may be non-normal, the views may involve nonlinear quantities,
and the constraints may be equalities or inequalities.

In numerical applications, the method can be thought of as performing
three steps:

$$\text{prior scenarios}
\quad\rightarrow\quad
\text{express views as constraints}
\quad\rightarrow\quad
\text{reweight scenarios}$$

Once the new probabilities are available, any statistic that was
previously computed with $p$ can instead be computed using the posterior
weights.

For a generic scenario-dependent quantity $z_j$, for example,

$$\mathbb E_p[Z]
=
\sum_{j=1}^J p_jz_j$$

becomes

$$\mathbb E_{p_c}[Z]
=
\sum_{j=1}^J p_{c,j}z_j.$$

The same idea extends naturally to portfolio returns, moments, risk
measures, and optimization problems.

Entropy Pooling therefore provides a bridge between two sources of
information:

$$\text{what the prior model says}
+
\text{what the investor believes}$$

without requiring either one to be discarded.

21(10), 97--102.
